What to Watch for in the 2026 U.S. Midterms

Nieman Reports · 2026-10-27 15:19 UTC

With the first U.S. midterm elections since President Donald Trump’s return to the White House approaching, voters will be weighing in on a range of issues, from the economy and rising cost of living, to the administration’s foreign policy and the future direction of both major parties. At a recent virtual Nieman-to-Nieman seminar, a group of Nieman alums who cover politics discussed what they’re hearing from voters with regards to key Senate races, the growing influence of younger voters drawn to progressive candidates, and the political implications of conflicts involving Iran, Ukraine, and Russia. Moderated by Austin Bogues (NF ’21), news desk editor at USA Today, the discussion brought together James Barragán (NF ’24), political anchor for Spectrum News in Austin, Texas; Bill Barrow (NF ’22), national politics reporter for The Associated Press in Atlanta; and Ines Pohl (NF ’05), Washington bureau chief and White House correspondent for Deutsche Welle, Germany’s international public broadcaster.

India Targets Journalists in Crackdown on Growing Protest Movement

Nieman Reports · 2026-10-19 21:20 UTC

As protests continue across India over allegations of government corruption, dozens of members of the media have been subjected to arrest, detainment and assault, according to witnesses, press rights organizations, and the journalists themselves. Thousands of protesters have taken to the streets of New Delhi in recent weeks, demanding the resignation of election officials allegedly tied to the deletion of nearly 130 million names from voter registration rolls. The protests — which have largely been organized by the Cockroach Janata Party, so named after India's chief justice called the nation’s unemployed youth and activists "cockroaches" — are part of a wider wave of youth discontent aimed at Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his administration. Organizers have mobilized young people via social media, tapping into frustrations with government corruption, eroding trust in democratic institutions, and a lack of access to jobs and educational opportunities.

Testing the Legal Limits of Press Access

Nieman Reports · 2026-10-15 14:51 UTC

The Trump administration’s latest attacks on the news media have followed a familiar pattern: President Donald Trump lashes out at news outlets for perceived bias and follows up with restrictive actions that appear blatantly unconstitutional; a judge’s ruling follows, temporarily halting the actions; and the administration pivots and pushes ahead with other restrictions. This time it was the removal of three outlets — CNN, MS NOW, and Politico — from White House press access in September. After the groups sued, and U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly issued a temporary restraining order restoring their access on Sept. 24, the administration barred CNN and Politico from providing pool coverage on trips outside Washington. Kelly issued a longer, preliminary injunction on Oct. 14, halting the administration from blocking the news organizations’ access to the White House while the case proceeds. This Newsroom Wants You to Be Part of the Journey Before It Even Starts

Nieman Reports · 2026-10-06 10:00 UTC

My happiest times in journalism have been when I have built something new. For my latest venture, I want to help bring investigative journalism on climate and environmental issues to a much larger audience than it has reached in the past. To do so, I’m starting a brand-new newsroom focused on the environmental and climate crisis, and I’m taking my audience along for the ride. I’ll be documenting every facet of the process with an “open kitchen” approach of radical transparency, starting with a 100-day video countdown chronicling all the steps involved with starting a news organization from the ground up. This effort combines two of the things I’m most passionate about: I love digging up stories that other people don’t want to see published, and I love creating opportunities for other journalists. I’ve been a journalist for most of my life. I started working at age 14 for the local paper in my rural German town, turned to doing investigative stories in my early 20s, and later studied investigative journalism at the Columbia University Graduate School of Journalism in New York.

America’s Shrinking Local Newsrooms, Through a Photographer’s Lens

Nieman Reports · 2026-10-02 12:30 UTC

For many journalists, the sight of empty desks is a sadly familiar one. My first glimpse of a gutted newsroom facing further cutbacks sparked a documentary photography project that has so far taken me to more than 50 newsrooms across the United States over the past eight years. It began when my mother, a loyal subscriber to our local metro in southern Illinois, told me a decade ago how disappointed she was in the newspaper. She complained that the local coverage was lacking, and the paper seemed to be thinner. Already several years into my photojournalism career, I was unsurprised by her remarks — I had been witnessing the decline of print media since graduation from journalism school. Still, my curiosity was piqued, and I arranged a visit to the paper to see for myself. Cue the scene of a barren newsroom. Not only were there empty desks, but also an expanse of exposed carpet with indentations showing where desks had once long stood. While there has been a great deal of reporting on the issues plaguing local journalism, I hadn’t seen the story told visually.

Seven Takeaways on Convenience and News

Nieman Reports · 2026-09-25 14:53 UTC

"Against Convenience: Embracing Friction in an Age of Endless Ease" was released on Sept.15, 2026, by Hanover Square Press, an imprint of HarperCollins Publishers. Courtesy of Hanover Square Press From the earliest pitch, I knew that I wanted to cover the news industry in my book, “Against Convenience.” The book looks at the technology around us and asks whether it’s really improving our lives. Is delivery food worth the higher price? Is streaming music better than collecting CDs or MP3s? News embodies the paradox of modern convenience: We have access to more information than ever before, but misinformation and partisanship are rampant and the purveyors of reliable information are struggling to stay solvent. Plus, I figured if I was going to criticize other fields — tech, entertainment, appliance manufacturing — I couldn’t avoid my own. I don’t know how interested the average nonjournalist is in the day-to-day operations of the news business, so I tried to look in the mirror more than gaze at my navel.

澳枪击事件嫌疑人为父子：曾宣誓效忠“伊斯兰国”，行凶枪支为合法持有

The Paper 澎湃新闻 · 2025-12-16 02:23 UTC

据新华社12月15日援引澳大利亚广播公司报道，澳大利亚联合反恐小组调查人员表示，悉尼邦迪滩枪击事件两名嫌疑人曾宣誓效忠“伊斯兰国”恐怖组织。 报道援引联合反恐小组一名不愿透露姓名的高级官员的话说，警方在邦迪滩两名枪手车内发现一面“伊斯兰国”旗帜。澳大利亚安全情报组织6年前就已在调查邦迪滩枪击案两名枪手之一的纳维德·阿克拉姆，他与“伊斯兰国”在悉尼的恐怖分子有密切联系。 澳大利亚警方表示，枪击事件的两名嫌疑人是父子关系，使用合法获得的枪支发动了此次袭击事件。 澳大利亚总理阿尔巴尼斯15日表示：“今天下午4点， 我将把更严格的枪支法律列入国家内阁的议程，包括限制个人可持有或许可的枪支数量 。此外，还需对许可证进行定期审查。人们的情况会发生变化，人们的思想也会随着时间的推移而变得激进。许可证不应永久有效。” 此次枪击事件已造成包括1名作案嫌疑人在内的16人死亡、40人受伤。这是自1996年塔斯马尼亚州亚瑟港枪击事件造成35人死亡以来，澳大利亚发生的最严重的大规模枪击事件。 持有枪支许可证长达十年 据多家外媒报道，其中一名袭击者为24岁的澳大利亚公民纳维德·阿克拉姆，他在现场被捕，随后被送往悉尼的一家医院。另一名袭击者是他的父亲萨吉德·阿克拉姆，他于1998年来到澳大利亚，被警方当场击毙。 澳大利亚警方随后证实，纳维德·阿克拉姆此前已被新南威尔士州警方和其他机构记录在案。其父亲萨吉德·阿克拉姆持有枪支许可证，名下登记有6支枪，目前均已被追回。新南威尔士州警察局长马尔·兰永透露，萨吉德·阿克拉姆已持有枪支许可证长达十年。 阿尔巴尼斯在新闻发布会上透露，纳维德·阿克拉姆曾于2019年10月首次引起当局的注意。他补充说，对该男子进行检查是基于他与其他人有联系，但评估结果表明，没有任何迹象表明他存在持续的威胁或暴力倾向。 新南威尔士州州长克里斯·明斯表示，警方正在调查他们的系统是否存在故障，导致合法持有的武器可能被用于恐怖袭击。 枪手“性格古怪”，爱好打猎 据《卫报》澳大利亚版报道，纳维德·阿克拉姆在袭击前从事砌砖工作。他的同事表示，纳维德性格古怪，“没人和他亲近”。“（砌砖工人）在一起的时间很长，因为砌砖是一项非常枯燥乏味的工作，所以大家会聊很多话。但纳维德是一个性格很古怪的人……他工作非常努力，几乎没有休息日。” 尽管澳大利亚警方并未确认纳维德·阿克拉姆是否合法持有枪支，但据这位同事表示，纳维德经常外出打猎，曾提及在昆士兰州南部高原的克鲁克韦尔附近射杀兔子和其他猎物。这位同事还表示，就在几周前，纳维德告诉老板，他的手骨折了，所以要到2026年才能工作。

儿童手表“小天才圈”调查：点赞成每日功课，有商家可解除家长管控

The Paper 澎湃新闻 · 2025-12-15 14:23 UTC

在校园里，孩子们时常举起戴在手腕上的手表，彼此一碰，便加为好友。 这种以“安全”为核心卖点的儿童电话手表，如今已超越通信工具的属性，悄然演变成一个拥有独特规则、社交层级甚至灰色产业链的未成年人数字社交圈——“小天才圈”。 在这个属于他们的“江湖”里，“大佬榜”备受关注，“扩列”（增加好友）成为新的社交需求，“点主”（在主页点赞）是每日必做的功课……这些让成年人感到陌生的词汇，正构筑着未成年人的数字社交世界。 然而，伴随着这种社交形态的兴起，家长们的担忧也日益加剧：孩子过度沉迷手表社交、不良信息传播、因品牌壁垒导致的“社交绑架”等问题逐渐浮现。《法治日报》记者近日对该现象展开调查，试图揭开这一未成年人数字社交圈的真实面貌。 点赞成社交“硬通货” 据北京“小天才圈”资深玩家陈曦（化名）介绍，圈内有5000余名活跃用户，多为11岁至17岁的学生，这个社交圈形成了一套精心设计的“混圈规则”。“入圈”需设定两个字的独特圈名，随后可在平台分享生活点滴，吸引具有相同爱好的好友进行互动；若想提升知名度或影响力，需每日经营主页并与好友动态互动。 记者注意到，在一些社交平台上，大量以“小天才圈交友攻略”为主题的内容应运而生，内容涵盖如何快速“扩列”、获取更多点赞等“实用”技巧，评论区有不少“留下ID互加好友”的留言。在这一社交体系中，点赞是这套规则的核心——平台设定每日主页获赞上限为3000个，若要达到“100万+”的“大佬”级别，需连续点赞近一年时间。围绕点赞数与知名度，圈内形成了清晰的“大佬排行榜”，点赞数也成为社交“硬通货”。 这种对点赞的追逐，已催生出相关服务产业。记者调查发现，某社交平台上，拥有数十万甚至上百万点赞数的账号，售价从几百元到上千元不等：100多万点赞的账号标价1300元，90多万点赞的账号标价1200元。 今年18岁的“灵师”（圈名），在2021年14岁时加入“小天才圈”，她的账号目前已拥有150个好友、超100万点赞量。她告诉记者，这样的账号市场价值约1000元。 “围绕点赞需求，还衍生出代刷赞、租账号、出售‘大佬好友位’等服务。”“灵师”进一步介绍，例如付费100元至180元，即可获得“bot”（记者注：“bot”是一种第三方开发的自动化工具，主要用于刷赞、修改记录和发送动态等功能，这类工具能帮助用户快速提升账号点赞数，从而在未成年人社交圈中获得更高地位）自动点赞功能——用户将手表寄给相关人员进行10天左右的处理便能完成安装。此后，发帖5分钟内即可自动获赞，还可以一键查询未点赞名单。

产地造假、年份速成、无视监管！央视曝光新会陈皮市场乱象

The Paper 澎湃新闻 · 2025-12-15 08:23 UTC

近日，总台接到群众举报，反映陈皮市场存在年份虚标、产地及工艺造假等问题，千元一斤的“年份陈皮”亦可能名不副实。 茶枝柑新果皮冒充陈皮 广西浦北出现“速成工艺陈皮” 记者发现，直播间里售卖陈皮低价轮番轰炸，年份承诺掷地有声。 直播间也有主播爆料，八成市面上所谓广东新会陈皮实为广西陈皮。 广西钦州市浦北县是茶枝柑重要种植基地，其果皮是陈皮风味“越陈越香”关键，也是浦北陈皮唯一原料。2024年当地陈皮产业产值破60亿元，采收季大量鲜果加工晾晒成柑皮。 果农和收购商称，今年浦北茶枝柑鲜果收购价走低。按20斤鲜果出1斤柑皮比例，叠加人工成本，品相好的新柑皮成本约30元/斤，低端柑皮仅六七元，且当年新柑皮并非真正陈皮。 这家企业的负责人告诉记者，按行业共识与团体标准，柑皮需陈化三年以上才可称为陈皮，陈化时间越长价值越高，但他透露，自然陈化需长期积压资金，多数企业是难以承受的。 这家企业的负责人私下告诉记者，为缓解资金占用压力，一种名为“轻工艺”的速成加工方式，眼下正在部分陈皮生产企业里流行，他们仅需一个月的时间，就能将新采收的茶枝柑果皮处理为外观近似三年、五年自然陈化过的陈皮，这样做能大幅缩短陈化周期、降低企业的运营成本。 浦北自然陈化五年陈皮批发价每斤150元至200元，企业造假“工艺皮”成本仅70元左右，高额利润促使更多商家放弃自然陈化、铤而走险。 记者离开企业，在广西浦北县柑浦堂健康产业有限公司分拣车间，再次见到大批量造假“工艺皮”陈皮，同一批“工艺皮”因加工受热差异形成色差，被分拣标注为三年、五年等不同年份。 负责人透露，不同年份“工艺皮”本质相同，批发价均70元左右一斤，零售价差极大，标五年款卖500元一斤，标十年款卖1000元一斤，仅凭外观就能翻倍抬价，利润超成本十倍以上。 新会陈皮从浦北进货 “工艺皮”贴上陈皮标签以假乱真 浦北与新会陈皮原料同为茶枝柑，仅产地不同，新会较高生产成本使当地部分头部商家常年从浦北拿货，浦北成其重要原料供应地。 记者在柑浦堂分拣仓库看到，大量标注“新会陈皮”“新会特产”的纸箱正打包“工艺皮”，这些广西陈皮每日批量发往广东新会，造假供需链路已成熟稳定。 记者发现，浦北当地部分规模企业和小型收购商，已形成了这种“工艺皮”的造假供应体系，可自主加工或快速调配各类“年份”陈皮货品，个别企业年销新会原料数量惊人。 随后经浦北陈皮企业负责人引荐，记者见到多位专程从新会赴浦北采购的商家，他们坦言同时经营新会皮与浦北皮，外地“工艺皮”因价格低廉成电商供货重要选择。

《怦然心动》导演莱纳与妻子在家中遇害，警方尚未证实是其子所杀

The Paper 澎湃新闻 · 2025-12-15 07:23 UTC

当地时间12月14日，曾执导《怦然心动》《当哈利遇到莎莉》《危情十日》等影片的美国导演罗伯·莱纳（Rob Reiner）在他位于洛杉矶的家中遇害身亡。洛杉矶警察已对外证实，现年78岁的莱纳与他现年68岁的妻子米歇尔·辛格·莱纳（Michele Singer Reiner）的遗体一同被发现。 2019年，罗伯·莱纳（左一）与《当哈利遇到莎莉》的主演梅格·瑞恩、比利·克里斯托出席TMC经典电影节。 据悉，洛杉矶消防局的人员于当地时间12月14日下午3点38分接到医疗救助电话，赶赴位于布伦特伍德区的一处住宅中，随后发现两人已死亡。当天晚间，洛杉矶警察局在其社交媒体官方账号确认死者为导演罗伯·莱纳夫妇，将由抢劫凶杀部门主导调查。而好莱坞媒体TMZ援引执法部门消息称，“两人身上有与刀具造成的伤口相符的割裂伤。” 好莱坞媒体《每日野兽》称，有消息人士向他们透露，是两人的女儿罗米最先发现他们倒在血泊中；罗伯·莱纳当时已死亡，妻子米歇尔在救护车送院途中离世。 此外，《人物》杂志称通过多方消息，得知莱纳夫妇系被他们的儿子尼克（Nick）所杀害。不过，这一说法并未获得警方的证实。罗伯·莱纳与摄影师米歇尔·辛格相识于《当哈利遇到莎莉》拍摄时期，两人于1989 年结婚，育有三个子女，分别为杰克（Jake）、尼克（Nick）和罗米（Romy）。 2014年，罗伯·莱纳与妻子偕三名子女杰克、罗米、尼克（右三至右一）出席活动。 《人物》杂志还在报道中指出：尼克2016年接受其采访时，曾谈到自己长达数年的毒品成瘾经历。这段经历始于他十几岁出头，导致他一度流落街头。他表示，大约从15岁开始，便反复进出戒毒康复机构；随着成瘾问题不断加重，他逐渐与家人疏远，并在多个州经历了长时间的无家可归生活。 2025年9月15日，罗伯·莱纳在纽约出席活动。视觉中国 图 获取更多RSS： https://feedx.net https://feedx.site

演员何晴追悼会举行，其子追思母亲：北京这场雪像是为她而下

The Paper 澎湃新闻 · 2025-12-15 06:53 UTC

一场雪落，人间倩影化雪归天。 12月15日上午，众多剧迷粉丝冒着严寒赶到北京昌平殡仪馆久安厅，送别演员何晴最后一程。12月13日，这位被誉为“古典第一美人”的演员因病去世，终年61岁。 不到10点，殡仪馆告别厅外已经站满了前来悼念的观众和粉丝，有人胸前佩戴小白花，有人手捧鲜花，一位浙江的网友还托人送来了悼念花圈。 “何晴的作品在我们心中留下了太多美好回忆，她的演技和性格都让我们深深喜爱，这次听到她突然去世的消息，我们非常意外，来到这里也是一种悼念。”一位何晴的影迷说。 现场粉丝在悼念簿上写下对何晴的话，不到一会儿，悼念簿就已写满对她的怀念。一位观众用清秀的字迹写下：“亲爱的何晴，我们的童年、青春都在您的影视作品中得到陪伴。美丽可人的何晴，很痛心听到您的消息，我代表我的同学们来这为你送行。” 曾在电视剧《水浒传》中饰演卢俊义的演员王卫国也来到现场，神色哀切。他说自己和何晴既是邻居，也是多年好友，在他印象中何晴是一个温婉、暖心的人，没有架子，总是远远地和人打招，笑嘻嘻地说话。何晴生病时常给王卫国打电话，请他送自己去医院。即便病重时，何晴也保持乐观积极的态度，王卫国有些事情想不开，她还来开导自己。“何晴走了，我们都很难过。只要你记住她，她就永远还在。”王卫国说。 《水浒传》中卢俊义的扮演者王卫国 《西游记》中万圣公主扮演者张青深情回忆何晴往事：“我们是小时候就认识的好朋友，从80年代到现在，有缘分做了这些年的朋友。她说话慢慢的，很甜很温柔。” 《西游记》中万圣公主扮演者张青 在广大观众的真挚请求下，原本仅面向亲友的告别仪式临时对外开放，大家排着队，秩序井然地进入灵堂，与这位“荧屏中的温婉佳人、生活中的坚韧女性”做最后的道别。 久安厅内的屏幕上滚动播放着何晴的照片，厅内四周摆满了亲友的花圈，其中包括六小龄童、唐国强、翁虹、尤勇智等何晴圈内好友送来的花圈，还有《三国演义》剧组送来的花圈。人群中不时传来一阵抽泣。 何晴之子许何代表亲友致悼词。他回忆了何晴对抗病魔的乐观积极，以及作为母亲对孩子深深的爱和眷恋。 许何说，妈妈很喜欢下雪，经常在雪后穿一件毛茸茸的衣服外出赏雪。“今年12月12日北京下了第一场雪，我摸着妈妈的脸跟她说北京下雪了，下得好大，好像很久都没有下过这么大的雪。在我的心里，这场雪好像是刻意为她下的。12月13日早晨天空晴朗，白色的雪布满了大地，我妈妈在她最喜欢的早晨离开了大家，去了天国，远离了所有的疾病和痛苦。” 何晴，1964年1月13日出生于浙江衢州江山市。她是中国内地唯一一位演遍四大名著影视作品的女演员，被誉为“古典第一美女”。

Growth of hybrid electric vehicle sales has slowed this quarter as the average transaction price for a new vehicle passed $50,000-the first time this price has been reached so far this year, according to Kelley Blue Book.

Easy money does not win elections

CEPR VoxEU · 2026-11-05 00:00 UTC

Politicians have long pressed central banks for lower interest rates in the belief that easy money wins elections. This column tests that premise using 385 parliamentary and presidential elections in 18 countries between 1900 and 2020. It finds no evidence that easy money helps incumbents. The most likely electoral return to a typical easing is close to zero, and large returns are ruled out. A modest return can be decisive only in exceptionally close races. The electoral case for pressing central banks is weak.

newspaper_magazine · generalist · R4 · P4 · baseline

Monetary policy in times of high public debt

CEPR VoxEU · 2026-11-05 00:00 UTC

High public debt around the globe has revived concerns that it could undo central banks’ ability to control inflation. Higher debt can lead to higher spending and increase inflation if households do not fully save debt-financed transfers. This column argues that central banks can still control inflation in these situations, but they must act following increases in debt levels and before they translate into higher inflation. Crucially, central banks should take into account that higher public debt increases the level of interest rates consistent with price stability.

Bank executive pay: Compensation design can help reduce excessive risk-taking

CEPR VoxEU · 2026-11-04 00:00 UTC

Bankers may benefit from the upside of risk-taking through bonuses, while taxpayers may ultimately bear the costs when things go badly wrong. After the Global Financial Crisis, regulators set out to change how bank executives are paid. This column examines how compensation practices have evolved since then and how they relate to bank risk. Longer deferral horizons, as mandated in the EU, have reduced bank risk-taking, but evidence on bonus caps is inconclusive. The 2023 banking turmoil shows that bank boards and supervisors play a crucial role in ensuring good governance of compensation frameworks.

Job seekers’ beliefs and preferences over wages and benefits: Experimental evidence from online job boards

CEPR VoxEU · 2026-11-04 00:00 UTC

From employer wage-setting power to the consequences of pay transparency and the role of benefits in compensation inequality, many core questions about labour markets hinge on how job seekers respond to wage and benefit differences across job ads. Combining a field experiment on over 100 Swiss job boards with a survey, this column shows that workers are imperfectly informed about wage and benefit differences across jobs. Posting wages redirects search towards better-paying jobs. Workers also value certain benefits highly – notably company cars and the option to work from home. Since higher-paying jobs tend to offer more benefits, inequality in job value exceeds wage inequality across jobs.

Repo is the new dollar safe asset

CEPR VoxEU · 2026-11-03 00:00 UTC

US Treasuries have long been the benchmark dollar safe asset, and the convenience yield they command is the price the world pays for dollar liquidity. This column shows that the convenience yield on ten-year Treasuries relative to corporate bonds has collapsed from around 60 to 10 basis points since 2019, while the premium on repo has held near 90. Repo, not the Treasury, is now the highest-convenience dollar safe asset. The same shift helps explain why the dollar has been losing ground as the global reserve asset even as domestic convenience yields hold up.

A network approach to geopolitics

CEPR VoxEU · 2026-11-03 00:00 UTC

In international affairs, what a country does depends on its own interests and on what its partners do. This column uses data on political institutions and UN voting to recover the network of geopolitical influence. The network tracks major shifts in international politics since the 1960s and reveals three notions of power: autonomy, control, and the ability to shape the game. Across all countries, the US has the most autonomy but China has the most control. Domestic political change in the US or China moves other countries the most, as the network transmits it furthest.

Can Home Visits Re-Engage Chronically Absent Students? Evidence from the LEAP Program -- by Eric Brunner, Shangyue Jiang, Stephen Ross

NBER · Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知

Beginning in the summer of 2021, the state of Connecticut launched the Learner Engagement and Attendance Program (LEAP) where home visits by school personnel were conducted with students identified as chronically absent from Connecticut’s 15 most disadvantaged school districts. Home visits were designed to connect students and their families directly with teachers to foster strong connections. We use student-level data from 2021–22 through 2023-24 to estimate event studies of the effect of LEAP on student attendance, chronic absenteeism, disciplinary incidents, and student achievement. Utilizing models that address selection into treatment timing over student observable and unobservable attributes, we find that students who received the LEAP intervention experienced approximately a 4 to 5 percentage point increase in attendance rates, a 13 to 15 percentage point decline in chronic absenteeism, and a 3 to 5 percentage point decline in the number of disciplinary incidents.

institutional · primary · R5 · P5 · baseline

Unraveling the Cobweb of Global Imbalances: Drivers, Vulnerabilities and Adjustment Scenarios -- by Stefan Avdjiev, Kristin Forbes, Tsvetelina Nenova, Marjorie Santos

NBER · Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知

This paper analyses the evolution and drivers of the stock of global imbalances in order to assess associated vulnerabilities and potential adjustment scenarios. These imbalances have recently increased sharply, with a deterioration in the US net international investment position (NIIP) mirrored by NIIP improvements in most other major economies. We decompose these NIIP changes into their proximate drivers for a sample of 28 economies and find that financial factors (including valuation changes and investment income flows) are the primary drivers of global imbalances at both short and long horizons, while trade also plays a significant role (especially at long horizons). Valuation gains on international investment positions have supported economic growth in many countries since 2010, while also increasing their vulnerability to financial market adjustments.

institutional · primary · R5 · P5 · baseline

Affirmative Action, Faculty Productivity and Caste Interactions: Evidence from Engineering Colleges in India -- by Robert W. Fairlie, Saurabh Khanna, Prashant Loyalka, Gagandeep S. Sachdeva

NBER · Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知

Affirmative action programs are often criticized because of concerns that they result in lower worker productivity and efficiency losses. We study the relative productivity of workers benefiting from an aggressive affirmative action policy in a setting where hiring constraints are mandated upon employers and are typically likely to bind. In India, colleges are required to reserve approximately 50 percent of faculty hires for individuals from disadvantaged caste and social class groups. We collect and analyze data from a nationally representative sample of 50 engineering and technology colleges in India, some of which randomly assign students to classrooms. We find that reservation category faculty have lower levels of education, lower professorial ranks and fewer years of experience in academia than general category faculty who are not hired through reservations.

institutional · primary · R5 · P5 · baseline

Saving for the Machines -- by Jesús Fernández-Villaverde

NBER · Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知

When machines can perform a growing share of tasks, growth depends on two margins: how the task structure affects the returns to accumulating machines, and how strongly capital accumulation responds to those returns. I argue that, in a standard task model, capital supply governs the size of the growth boom associated with automation, while the task structure sets the duration of this growth boom and the evolution of wages. I document how the same technology path that generates 11.7% annual growth when households choose their saving rate optimally delivers only 2.2% when the saving rate is fixed at the calibrated U.S. 2025 level of 23%. Therefore, slow growth might reflect too little capital accumulation instead of a technological bottleneck. Also, the saving rate rises mainly because automation raises the capital share, not because households become thriftier. Long yields price the growth boom: the ten-year real yield jumps from 5.1% to 13.6% on impact.

institutional · primary · R5 · P5 · baseline

Income Inequality and Intergenerational Mobility in Russia: Trends, Sources, and Measurement -- by Kristina Butaeva, Steven N. Durlauf, Dmitry Rudenko

NBER · Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知

This chapter documents trends in income and inequality in Russia from the collapse of the Soviet Union through 2025, drawing on official statistics, the existing literature, and household survey microdata. It also reviews evidence on intergenerational mobility. While there is a consensus that inequality dramatically increased during the 1990s, its post-2000 trajectory is contested. Initial household survey studies usually found a decline, whereas official statistics reported a comparatively stable Gini coefficient. Our analysis of Russia's major household surveys, harmonized using common measurement conventions, aligns with the survey-based literature, indicating that the Gini coefficient generally fell from approximately 0.45–0.48 in the early 2000s to 0.29–0.38 in the early 2020s. We further find that most inequality arises within rather than between regions, urban and rural areas, and education and occupation groups. Household labor-market attachment, region, and household composition account for the largest shares of the explained variance in log income.

institutional · primary · R5 · P5 · baseline

Public R&D and the Automation of Manufacturing: Evidence from the Space Race -- by Apoorva Babbar, Shawn Kantor, Alexander Whalley, Jingyuan Zeng

NBER · Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知

This paper examines how public research and development shaped the direction of technological change during the Cold War–era Space Race and its consequences for US manufacturing. While prior research has documented the effects of public R&D on innovation and economic growth, less is known about whether mission-oriented public investment directed innovation toward automation and how this affected labor markets. We exploit variation in exposure to NASA's Space Race investments across industries and locations to estimate the effects of public R&D on innovation and manufacturing outcomes from 1947 to 1992. Combining newly developed measures of automation in full-text patent data with historical evidence on government involvement in patenting, we show that NASA-sponsored patents are systematically more automation-intensive than non-NASA patents within the same technological classes. Industries and locations more exposed to Space Race activity experienced persistent declines in labor share, consistent with the diffusion of labor-saving technologies developed for space applications.

LLM Intelligence, measured by Starburst, has been basically linear over time since that start of the reasoning era. By Chapin Lenthall-Cleary and Cole Gaboriault In summer 2024, my friend Cole and I started a hobby research program into perceptions of (human) intelligence. We started by creating a bespoke 1-5 intelligence scale[1] and rating people we knew. Our plan was to then make a bunch of tests, give them to the people we rated, and see which tests, if any, correlated with our ratings. One of those tests was Starburst. We’ve talked about it before; in short, it’s a puzzle game where one tries to figure out the laws of physics of a fictional universe. We never did get very many people to play it. But using the results of two early playthroughs (Cole’s and our friend Ryan’s), some further test playthroughs where we pretended to be people of certain intelligences, some a priori reasoning about which parts of the game would be difficult, and a healthy dose of raw intuition, we pieced together a correspondence between Starburst scores and our intelligence scale.

3 original methods for measuring the distance to the stars

Big Think · 2026-11-05 07:00 UTC

Out there in space, blazing just a scant 150 million kilometers away lies the brightest and most massive object in our Solar System: the Sun. Shining hundreds of thousands of times as bright in Earth’s skies as the next brightest object, the full Moon, the Sun is unique among Solar System objects for producing its own visible light, rather than only appearing illuminated because of reflected light. However, the thousands upon thousands of stars visible in the night sky — escalating into the millions and billions when we aid our vision with telescopes and cameras — are all also self-luminous, distinguishing themselves from the planets and other Solar System objects in that regard. But how far away are they? Unlike the planets, Sun, and Moon, the stars appear to remain fixed in their position over time: not only from night-to-night but also throughout the year and even from year-to-year. We even call it “the fixed background of stars” when measuring the motion of objects within our Solar System against them.

J-lens preferentially reads from coordinate-aligned subspaces

LessWrong · 2026-11-05 03:31 UTC

Note: I only test on Gemma-4-31B, which contains the spaces I've been studying in this earlier post. This is a shorter post, with just a few observations potentially relevant to those working on the J-lens work. The main observations here are: In Gemma-4, there are two relatively small subspaces that account the majority of the J-lens readout. These are both coordinate-aligned subspaces. That means we can take a hidden state, mask out all coordinates except both these ~600 coordinate groups, and it will capture ~80-95% of the J-lens readout. These spaces are not built to capture J-lens contribution. Both spaces are defined by a distinctive pattern in the weights: the post-norm diagonal is very small on these coordinates. That is, the space is protected from edits for many consecutive layers. Nonetheless, semantically valuable information often still exists outside these spaces, complicating an overly clean isolated 'workspace' story. The more you know, the harder it is to change someone’s mind

Big Think · 2026-11-04 16:00 UTC

Here’s the bad news: The deeper your understanding of an issue and the stronger your conviction about the solution, the worse you often become at persuasion. This isn’t a character flaw; it’s a law of neuroscience. Once you understand it, you’ll stop wondering why your brilliant ideas and proposals keep floundering in meeting rooms. It’s due to a cognitive trap that the fields of behavioral economics and neuroscience have spent decades documenting: the curse of knowledge. Once I explain how it works, you’ll start to recognize why it’s working against your persuasion. In the early 1990s, Stanford graduate student Elizabeth Newton designed a simple experiment that revealed something profound about human cognition. She divided participants into two groups: “tappers” and “listeners.” Tappers were given a list of well-known songs like “Happy Birthday to You” and “The Star-Spangled Banner” — simple tunes everyone knows. They were asked to tap out a song’s rhythm on a table while a listener tried to identify it.

A fake Einstein quote actually explains the affordability crisis

Big Think · 2026-11-04 07:00 UTC

One of the most famous quotes commonly attributed to Einstein was something that he himself never actually said: “Compound interest is the eighth wonder of the world. He who understands it, earns it; he who doesn’t, pays it.” While the quote is not from Einstein at all, the math behind the concept of compound interest is incredibly profound, playing a role in any system — physical, mathematical, or financial — that accumulates based on how much of a base amount is present. When the base amount increases, it isn’t just the original amount (the principal) that continues to accumulate, but the additional amount (the interest) that adds to the accumulation as well. While investors most often use this to explain the growth of wealth in an interest-bearing account, it can be applied not just to wealth, but to the cost and price of goods and commodities that continue to increase over time as well. When wealth increases, we call it compound interest, but when prices increase, we call it inflation: not the cosmic kind, but the economic kind.

Mapping the brain won’t unlock all its secrets. That’s a good thing.

Big Think · 2026-11-03 15:30 UTC

There’s a quote attributed to New Zealand physicist Ernest Rutherford that goes something like this: “All science is either physics or stamp collecting.” In other words, some scientists perform experiments to explain how things work, while others don’t test specific hypotheses but instead observe the natural world and take note of what they find. The latter may seem inferior, but don’t underestimate the influence of observational science; after all, biology’s greatest stamp collector was probably Charles Darwin, who planted the seeds of his theory of evolution by natural selection in his detailed field journal published in 1839: The Voyage of the Beagle. In neuroscience, two types of stamp collections — wiring diagrams, or connectomes, and parts lists, or cell type atlases — are a major focus of time, effort, and financial investment. For example, the adult Drosophila connectome, published on a website called FlyWire.ai, is freely available for anyone to peruse.

Neuropsychiatrist Iain McGilchrist has spent over three decades studying how the brain’s two hemispheres shape consciousness, and says almost everything we think we know about them is wrong. What natural object is the roundest in the Universe?

Big Think · 2026-11-03 07:00 UTC

Here on planet Earth, we normally think of our own home world as round, and yet it’s anything but a perfect sphere. If it were made of a perfect fluid, didn’t rotate, and completely isolated from other masses that exert tidal forces on it (like the Sun and the Moon), it would be theoretically be massive enough to pull itself into a perfectly spherical shape, but that doesn’t line up with physical reality. The Earth instead is made of non-uniform material, has several interior layers that subduct and uplift, and is flattened into an oblate spheroidal shape: compressed at the poles and bulging at the equator. All told, the peak of Chimborazo in Ecuador is farthest from Earth’s center at 6384.4 kilometers, while the geographic North Pole in the Arctic Ocean is the closest point on the atmospheric surface at just 6356.77 kilometers away. All told, that means that Earth is “only” a sphere to a precision of 99.57%, with an 0.43% departure from perfect sphericity.

Filmmaker Survey | Lance Hammer

MUBI Notebook · 2026-11-05 08:00 UTC

Juliette Binoche and Tom Courtenay in Queen at Sea (Lance Hammer, 2026). With Queen at Sea (2026), American filmmaker Lance Hammer returns to direct his second film nearly two decades after his remarkable debut Ballast, which won the Grand Jury and directing awards at Sundance in 2008. Premiering in competition at the Berlin International Film Festival, the new film deservedly took home awards for Hammer’s direction and for actors Anna Calder-Marshall and Tom Courtenay, who play a long-married elderly couple. Leslie (Calder-Marshall), who suffers from dementia, is cared for at home by her husband Martin (Courtenay), who intentionally continues their sexual relationship even after it seems like his wife cannot consciously consent. When caught and confronted by Amanda (Juliette Binoche), Leslie’s daughter and Martin’s stepdaughter, he defends his actions as acts of love that offers his wife succor.

Can This Be Dixie?: Building the Hollywood South

MUBI Notebook · 2026-11-03 08:00 UTC

Hallelujah (King Vidor, 1929). The American South exists only in the imagination, yet it’s as real as sin. It cannot merely be the land situated beneath the Mason-Dixon (the historical survey line that traditionally demarcated Northern and Southern states), whose citizens fought under the banner of the Confederacy; one cannot ignore the obviously Southern states of West Virginia and Kentucky, or the political split between West and East Tennessee. It cannot be a shared culture or a shared history, for the residents of Jacksonville, Florida, find little in common with those families tucked deep in the Appalachian hollers or those ruling the oil-rich cities of eastern Texas. It is not a nation with shared laws, beliefs, or even religions. Instead, as the writers of the region have long known, the American South is a series of stories that overlap, contradict, and play off each other.

At the 51st Toronto International Film Festival (TIFF), which saw the inaugural edition of its official content market, the atmosphere was unmistakably different from its jubilee year. The spirit of nostalgic celebration and victory lapping from 2025's "TIFFty" celebration had evaporated, leaving behind the gritty residue of cinema as a commercial product. Lacking the elegance of “Marché du Film” at Cannes and the specificity of “European Film Market” at Berlinale, for their new industry initiative TIFF settled on a name that evokes the absurdity of local hero Matt Johnson’s Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie (2025). Its sans-serif, all-lowercase stylization will transport some Canadians to the grocery aisle, recalling Loblaws mogul Galen Weston’s “No Name” brand, a proudly generic grocery chain that prides itself on serving its customer base during tough economic times (while price-gouging them to death). “TIFF: The Market” attempted to do the same, stimulating the global screen sector amid layoffs and mergers through a $16.

Jerónimo Quevedo is an Argentine producer and the founder of Un Puma, a production company through which he has produced more than twenty short, medium-length, and feature films spanning fiction, documentary, and experimental cinema. He has worked with both established and emerging directors from Latin America and Europe, including Martín Rejtman, Teddy Williams, Affonso Uchoa, Konstantina Kotzamani, Ico Costa, and Thomas Woodroffe. His filmography is characterized by projects that embrace significant artistic risks and a strong authorial vision, helping to renew the paths of Latin American cinema through works such as Teddy Williams’s The Human Surge (2016), Vladimir Durán’s Goodbye Enthusiasm (2017), Manque La Banc’s Ski (2021), and. His films have been screened and recognized at festivals and events such as Cannes, Locarno, San Sebastián, Berlin, and Venice.

Wire mix: Inside Prepared Piano

The Wire Magazine · 2026-10-27 00:00 UTC

To accompany her feature in The Wire 513, Jo Hutton compiles an annotated mix of tracks that make use of prepared piano The piano can be prepared by placing objects such as pins, screws, bolts, crocodile clips, ball bearings, kitchen utensils, magnets or tin foil on or between the strings. Its history dates back at least to the 1930s, when choreographer Syvilla Fort commissioned a dance piece from John Cage, who proposed his Bacchanale for percussion ensemble. But the performance theatre was too small to fit the intended ensemble, so Cage changed the sound of the house piano by adding screws and objects inside it to make it more percussive. This annotated mix includes tracks by some of the artists Jo Hutton speaks to as part of her feature in The Wire 513, plus pieces from across the history of the prepared piano.

A Garden City in the Caribbean: Planning Belize’s New Capital, Belmopan

ArchDaily · 2026-11-05 04:00 UTC

Located on the Caribbean coast of Central America, Belize is a small country with an intriguing history. It is bordered by Mexico to the north and Guatemala to the west and south, with the Caribbean Sea along its eastern edge. Known as British Honduras for most of its past, it was formally made into a British colony in 1862, long after its Central American neighbors had won their independence from Spain. As the territory transitioned toward independence, it adopted two symbols of its emerging identity: a new name, Belize, and a new capital, which was built not just to govern the new nation, but also as a way to prevent hurricanes from putting the country's institutional stability at risk.

ArchDaily · 2026-11-05 03:00 UTC

Set on the gentle hillside of Khao Phra Tamnak, the house is conceived through a flexible design diagram rather than a predetermined architectural form. The project begins with the conditions of the place and the lives to be accommodated: a gradual change in land level, the family's need for generous and usable flat spaces, the principles of Feng Shui, and the presence of neighboring homes. These factors are not treated as separate constraints. They are brought together in a framework that can be tested, adjusted, and extended.

Homes Around Trees / architectureRED

ArchDaily · 2026-11-05 02:00 UTC

Urban housing in India stands at the intersection of rapid urbanization and a shifting sense of identity. The pressures of land scarcity and market-driven development have transformed housing into a commodity, often prioritizing maximum yield over the fundamental idea of home. In the process, the very essence of housing—as a space that fosters identity, community, and rootedness — is increasingly eroded. The relentless stacking of units, the erasure of open space, and the homogenization of urban environments leave little room for meaningful engagement with nature or with each other.

Rock Paper Shotgun · 2026-11-04 17:30 UTC

Long waits between mainline entries in a series aren’t a new phenomenon, if perhaps a bit more common nowadays due to big games' ballooning development cycles. It took about 23 years for BioWare’s Baldur's Gate 2 to be followed up by Larian’s Baldur’s Gate 3, though there were a decent amount of spin-offs and remasters peppered between the two. The wait for The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel hasn’t stretched on that long quite yet, but as Bethesda finally revealed concrete details about it just in time for Skyrim's 15th birthday, it really hit home for me that TES VI will be tasked with restoring motion to a world where calendars have been stuck in the 201st year of the 4th era since 2011. Perhaps it’s because I’m still in my twenties and haven’t lived long enough to see that many things I like pause their forward march for this long before returning.

Also, Naboo starfighters, if you really must. It's a total conversion of poor dead Volition's venerable dogfighter FreeSpace 2, running on the open source Free Space 2 Open engine via the popular Knossos launcher. You don't need a copy of FreeSpace 2 to play it. You also don't need to pay. journal · primary · R5 · P5 · reference

Core reduction for increasing neutron flux and radioisotope production in the IEA-R1 research reactor

arXiv · 2026-11-05 05:00 UTC

arXiv:2611.05409v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This work aims to present and analyze a new reactor core configuration for the IEA-R1 reactor core with the objective of enhancing its neutron irradiation capabilities. The reactor was modeled using the KENO-VI module from the SCALE Code System, provided by ORNL. Results have shown that implementing a near-cylindrical configuration with 20 fuel elements in the IEA-R1 core could substantially increase neutron flux, particularly in the center irradiation positions such as the EIBe (Beryllium Irradiated Element). After comparing various configurations, we conducted a brief analysis of the proposed core configuration's potential to produce 177Lu, resulting in a 34% increase in the specific activity of 177Lu considering a fuel power cycle around 21 days.

preprint · primary · R4 · P5 · signal

Holographic dark energy through Kruglov entropy

arXiv · 2026-11-05 05:00 UTC

arXiv:2611.05412v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study a holographic dark energy model built on the new entropy proposed by Kruglov, $S_K=S_{BH}/(1+\gamma S_{BH}^2)$, with the Granda--Oliveros infrared cutoff $L^{-2}=\alpha H^2+\beta\dot H$ in a flat universe. The Kruglov entropy is smaller than the Bekenstein--Hawking entropy and has a maximum value. We obtain the energy density of the model, the differential equation for the dark energy density parameter, and the expressions for the equation of state parameter, the deceleration parameter and the squared sound speed. At early times the model behaves like the usual Granda--Oliveros holographic dark energy, and the dark energy follows the background with a constant fraction. At late times the Kruglov correction gives a stable de Sitter future when $\alpha>1$, with the final Hubble rate fixed by the entropy parameter. The model gives a matter era followed by a dark energy era, with a transition from deceleration to acceleration near $z\approx0.66$.

preprint · primary · R4 · P5 · signal

Competition between tension and bending waves in a pre-stretched soft beam : experimental validation

arXiv · 2026-11-05 05:00 UTC

arXiv:2611.05414v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Competition between tension and bending waves in a pre-stretched soft beam Pre-stretched one-dimensional soft beams serve as an important and simplified model in mechanics, biomechanics, and soft material characterization. The propagation characteristics of transverse waves excited on such beams are commonly used to characterize elastic stiffness and tensile state. However, conventional pure beam or string models cannot fully explain the phase velocity dispersion of transverse waves in pre-stretched beams, particularly when the dispersion coexists with an increase in wave speed as tension increases. This frequency-dependent transition between tension-dominated and bending-dominated behavior has not yet been directly validated using measured dispersion curves in one-dimensional soft beams. Here, we use optical elastography, a high spatiotemporal resolution technique, to track transverse wave propagation in a soft incompressible cylinder under different tension levels and obtain the corresponding phase velocity dispersion curves.

preprint · primary · R4 · P5 · signal

A Unified Perspective on Poincar\'e and Galilei Relativity: II. General Relativity: A. Kinematics

arXiv · 2026-11-05 05:00 UTC

arXiv:2611.05425v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Building on the first paper in this series (Paper~I), a unified perspective on Poincar\'e and Galilei physics in a 5-dimensional spacetime setting is further pursued by consideration of the kinematics of general relativity, with the gravitational dynamics to be addressed separately. The metric of the 5-dimensional affine spacetimes governed by the Bargmann groups considered in Paper~I (central extensions of the Poincar\'e and Galilei groups) is generalized to curved spacetime by extending the usual 1+3 (traditionally `3+1') formalism of general relativity on 4-dimensional spacetime to a 1+3+1 formalism, whose spacetime kinematics is shown to be consistent with that of the usual 1+3 formalism.

How much data does a memory kernel need? Measurement requirements for fractional models of battery and corrosion degradation

arXiv · 2026-11-05 05:00 UTC

arXiv:2611.05426v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How much data does a memory kernel need before a fit is meaningful? For a distributed-order model, the answer is about 3.1 decades of observation, more than standard battery-degradation tests provide. Battery capacity fade and corrosion-film growth depend on their history, so they are often modelled using general fractional calculus (GFC), where memory is described by an arbitrary Sonine kernel rather than a single power law. We tested this using two mechanistic models without fractional operators and de Levie's porous-electrode model, whose high-frequency order is exactly 0.5; our estimator recovered 0.500. A single aging curve can recover an effective order, alpha, to within 5% noise using a weak formulation, while separating the tempered parameters (alpha, lambda) requires several Arrhenius conditions, with errors improving from (0.25, 0.43) with one condition to (0.04, 0.07) with four. A distributed-order memory needs 3.

preprint · primary · R4 · P5 · signal

Improving the performance of regularized Stokeslet simulations using Rosenbrock time integration methods

arXiv · 2026-11-05 05:00 UTC

arXiv:2611.05428v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The method of regularized Stokeslets (MRS) is widely used to model fluid-structure interactions of microscopic bodies in viscous environments. Specifically, MRS computes the fluid velocity generated by regularized forces distributed on an immersed body, which in turn defines a system of ordinary differential equations with which to evolve the body so that the no-slip condition is enforced. To accurately model material properties such as elasticity and bending rigidity, the resulting ODE system is often stiff and, therefore, computationally expensive to solve with explicit time-integration methods. Here we demonstrate the potential of linearly implicit Rosenbrock (ROS) time integration methods to greatly reduce the computational time required to solve such ODE systems. We focus on the classic model problem of the swimming of a flexible filament driven by preferred curvature forcing.

Nationwide trends in physical disability among rheumatoid arthritis patients in Korea (2010–2022): A retrospective cohort study based on national registry data

PLOS ONE Biology · 2026-11-04 14:00 UTC

by Bo Young Kim, Ji-Won Kim, Hwajeong Lee, Jung-Yoon Choe, Sung-Hoon Park, Sang Gyu Kwak Background Whether the burden of legally certified disability among patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA) has decreased in the modern treatment era is uncertain, particularly in Asia. We investigated trends in registered and physical disability among Korean patients with RA. Methods Using National Health Insurance Service data (patient-level 50% random sample), we identified patients aged ≥19 years with seropositive RA registered in the copayment assistance program for rare and intractable diseases in 2010–2022. Disability status, including physical disability (certified musculoskeletal impairment), came from the national disability registry. We estimated annual prevalence and, in newly diagnosed patients, incidence per 1,000 person-years, and compared the results with national disability statistics. Results The number of patients with seropositive RA identified in the database and included in this study was 33,992 in 2010 and 67,844 in 2022.

journal · primary · R4 · P4 · signal

Structural characteristics and policy differences of digital health management policies in China: A quantitative analysis based on the PMC index model

PLOS ONE Biology · 2026-11-04 14:00 UTC

by Tong Lyu Digital health governance increasingly relies on policy systems that coordinate data resources, information platforms, standards, service delivery, regulation, security, innovation, and implementation support. However, the structural composition and cross-policy heterogeneity of China’s national digital health policy system remain insufficiently quantified. This study develops a domain-specific Policy Modeling Consistency (PMC) framework to evaluate the structural coverage of national-level digital health management policies in China. Using a source-locked corpus covering 2016–2025, 42 eligible policies were identified, of which 39 with complete and auditable texts were included in the quantitative analysis. The framework comprises nine dimensions and 48 binary indicators, generating 1,872 policy-by-indicator coding decisions. An independently coded 11-policy subset yielded 96.78% agreement and a Cohen’s kappa of 0.914. The mean PMC score was 6.654 (SD = 1.456; median = 6.500; range = 3.467–9.000).

journal · primary · R4 · P4 · signal

Integrative analysis reveals shared biomarkers and pathways in osteoporosis and rheumatoid arthritis using machine learning and single-cell sequencing

PLOS ONE Biology · 2026-11-04 14:00 UTC

by Jin Zhao, Yixuan Chen, Fei Yang, Cheng Tian, Wenyan Luo, Zhou Su, Bohuan Yang, Wei Liu, Hongbo Yang Background Osteoporosis (OP) and Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA) are prevalent chronic diseases characterized by bone loss and immune dysregulation. Evidence suggests that patients with RA are at increased risk of developing OP; however, the shared molecular mechanisms linking these conditions remain incompletely understood. Methods Publicly available bulk transcriptomic and single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) datasets for OP and RA were obtained from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database. Weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) was applied to identify shared gene modules associated with both diseases. Functional enrichment and protein–protein interaction analyses were performed to characterize common biological pathways. Machine learning algorithms, including Random Forest (RF) and Support Vector Machine (SVM), were used to identify and validate shared hub genes and to construct diagnostic models.

Treadmill prehabilitation attenuates jejunal inflammation and enhances cytoprotective protein expression in murine gut ischemia–reperfusion

PLOS ONE Biology · 2026-11-04 14:00 UTC

by Kazuya Higashizono, Kazuya Takahashi, Kazuhiko Fukatsu, Tomonori Narita, Haruka Takayama, Midori Noguchi, Satoshi Murakoshi, Yasuyuki Seto Introduction Whether preoperative exercise protects the intestine itself is unclear. We hypothesized that treadmill prehabilitation acts on the intestine as ischemic preconditioning, and examined intestinal injury and cytokine responses after gut ischemia–reperfusion (I/R) and jejunal cytoprotective protein expression before ischemia. Methods Two experiments were conducted in male C57BL/6J mice. In Experiment 1, mice were randomly allocated to a sedentary or an exercise group; exercised mice completed 1 week of acclimation and 3 weeks of treadmill running. One day after the final session, the superior mesenteric artery was occluded for 45 min. Jejunal and ileal cytokines were measured in 24 mice, and mucosal injury was graded by the Chiu classification in 22 mice, at 3 or 6 h after reperfusion.

Spatial accessibility and equity of emergency medical services: Evidence from Ningbo

PLOS ONE Biology · 2026-11-04 14:00 UTC

by Minxia Fu, Jieyi Guan, Yixi Zheng, Xingchuan Gao, Wenwan Jin, Pengtao Wang Background Timely access to emergency medical services (EMS) is essential for improving survival outcomes and public health. In rapidly urbanizing Chinese cities, disparities in EMS accessibility are increasingly shaped by the spatial distribution of hospitals, population concentration, transport infrastructure, and built environment conditions. However, relatively few studies have simultaneously compared emergency and non-emergency medical accessibility and examined their spatial equity and influencing factors in medium-sized coastal cities. This study evaluates the spatial accessibility, equity, and clustering characteristics of EMS in Ningbo, China, and identifies the key built environment factors influencing these patterns. Methods The shortest travel time model, based on API data, was employed to measure EMS accessibility for both emergency (ambulance) and non-emergency (public transport) scenarios across five core urban districts of Ningbo.

journal · primary · R4 · P4 · signal

Simple and multiplexed tracking of bacterial growth in double emulsion droplets

PLOS ONE Biology · 2026-11-04 14:00 UTC

by Sebastián Somolinos Cedeño, Samuel Thompson, Polly Fordyce, Drew Endy Droplet-based microfluidics enable researchers to observe phenotypic heterogeneity within complex biological mixtures through parallel encapsulation of individual samples followed by imaging. Observing or quantifying dynamic heterogeneity remains challenging due to complexities associated with trapping and tracking many individual droplets. Current approaches for time-lapse imaging require specialized devices with droplet traps that limit accessibility and throughput. Here, using readily available materials and software, we demonstrate a simple method for stabilizing and monitoring many, individual droplets for up to 12 hours. We leveraged our method to track bacterial growth within droplets in a high-throughput manner for over 6 hours. Our method allows tracking the changes and variation in growth rate within and across droplets, revealing heterogeneity in growth patterns hidden in batch assays.

[Comment] Redefining curative treatment for early-stage mismatch repair-deficient colon cancer

The Lancet · Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知

For decades, the standard of care for patients with resected stage II and III colon cancer has centred on surgery with consideration of postoperative adjuvant systemic therapy to reduce risk of recurrence. Mismatch repair deficiency is seen in 10–15% of non-metastatic colon cancers and is predictive of response to immune checkpoint inhibition. The initial report of the single-arm, phase 2 NICHE-2 study of one dose of ipilimumab (1 mg per kg) and two doses of nivolumab (3 mg per kg) before surgery with clinical stage II and III colon cancer generated considerable interest after demonstrating a remarkable 98% pathologic response rate, including a pathologic complete response rate of 68%.

journal · primary · R5 · P5 · baseline

The Lancet · Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知

In patients with locally advanced dMMR colon cancer, treatment with ipilimumab and nivolumab before surgery resulted in a 3-year disease-free survival and 5-year overall survival of 100%. These findings support neoadjuvant nivolumab plus ipilimumab as a potential standard of care for patients with locally advanced dMMR colon cancer.

[Comment] Preserving the uterus: an effective dual therapy to avoid hysterectomy

The Lancet · Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知

Heavy menstrual bleeding is a challenging condition that, when refractory to conventional treatment, frequently culminates in hysterectomy. Endometrial ablation offers an effective, uterus-sparing alternative for women who do not desire future childbearing, with lower perioperative morbidity and faster recovery than hysterectomy.1–3 However, the durability of this procedure can be variable. Residual endometrium can result in recurrent bleeding or cyclical pelvic pain requiring further treatment, with approximately one in ten women undergoing hysterectomy within 2 years.

CRISPR tiling mutagenesis of the 10-kb human MYC locus mapped the fitness landscape of an entire human gene at base-pair resolution. This unbiased interrogation revealed that 67% of functionally essential base pairs are noncoding. An ultraconserved RNA regulatory element was identified that controls MYC localization and can be therapeutically targeted to suppress cancer cell growth in patient-derived tumor organoids.

Octopus and cuttlefish suckers may have evolved by repurposing ancient developmental genes

Phys.org Mollusks · 2026-10-20 13:30 UTC

Cephalopods, like the octopus, have specialized arms and suckers, but how these structures evolved from the simple bodies of their mollusk ancestors remains a mystery. Researchers from the University of Tokyo compared gene activity during embryonic development of cuttlefish, octopus and snail body parts. They found that several genes associated with appendage patterning showed expression along developing cephalopod arms, but no comparable patterns in developing suckers. Developing suckers instead expressed Ets1, a gene associated with early embryonic development in mollusks. The findings suggest cephalopods evolved suckers by reusing existing genes in new ways.

Think You Can Save The Hubble Space Telescope? NASA Wants To Know.

SoylentNews · Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知

"Arthur T Knackerbracket" writes: https://arstechnica.com/space/2026/10/think-you-can-save-the-hubble-space-telescope-nasa-wants-to-know/ The Hubble Space Telescope still shines in the eyes of astronomers after 36 years in orbit, but it is not as nimble as it once was. Left alone, the observatory will plunge back into the atmosphere in the early-to-mid-2030s, closing the book on one of the most famous scientific instruments of the century. NASA last raised the orbit of Hubble in 2002, when the Space Shuttle Columbia visited the observatory for a servicing mission. The final shuttle servicing flight in 2009 did not reboost the telescope's orbit, and with the retirement of the shuttle fleet two years later, Hubble has steadily lost altitude with no way to stave off eventual destruction. The space agency released a Request For Information (RFI) on Thursday asking commercial companies for ideas on how to reboost, service, or a controlled disposal of Hubble. Responses are due November 30.

Critical security vulnerability affects OpenSSH on Alpine Linux systems

LWN.net · 2026-11-05 11:39 UTC

Version 10.6p2 of OpenSSH has been released with a workaround for a critical vulnerability that affects Linux systems that use musl libc with PAM disabled, such as Alpine Linux. OpenSSH developer Damien Miller said: If you operate a Linux system that uses musl libc without PAM (Alpine Linux is one example) then stop reading and set PasswordAuthentication=no or disable SSH for these systems IMMEDIATELY. This vulnerability does not exist on non-Linux systems, Linux/glibc systems and Linux systems that use PAM for password authentication. We consider the root cause of this bug to be outside OpenSSH itself, but we're in a good position to deliver a mitigation quickly. The Alpine Linux project has announced that it will be backporting the OpenSSH fix "all the way back to Alpine 3.16", which was released in May 2022.

Researchers May Have Discovered the 6th Dwarf Planet

SoylentNews · Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知

"Arthur T Knackerbracket" writes: The other five are Pluto, Ceres, Eris, Haumea and Makemake: Space is vast, with trillions of objects in it, so it's not necessarily a surprise when scientists find new objects there, even if it's sometimes entirely by accident. Some objects are scarcer than others, and dwarf planets in our solar system are among the rarest, with only five recognized examples. A group of researchers from the Vera C. Rubin Observatory may have just found a sixth. Meet ED138, a dwarf planet candidate. It was found earlier in October when Rubin Operations team member Matthew Holman noted an unusually large object uncovered by a program he'd written with colleague Kevin Napier to scan Rubin Observatory data for moving objects. "My first reaction was one of excited disbelief," Holman said in a statement. "Objects like this are very rare, so I immediately started checking whether I or the code had done something wrong." Holman ran the search a second time through archived data and found the same object 20 more times dating back to March 2026.

[$] Portable Python scripts with dependencies

LWN.net · 2026-11-04 14:45 UTC

A basic Python script is portable: it can be copied between machines with little concern about compatibility. A script that depends on third-party packages requires quite a bit more care and consideration, however. In 2023, PEP 723 ("Inline script metadata") introduced a standard for declaring a Python script's dependencies inside the script itself. Several third-party tools can now automatically install and manage those dependencies, but there is still little official support for this standard within Python itself.

Qwen 3.8 27B on my laptop can interpret model weights, too

Simon Willison's Weblog · 2026-11-03 16:29 UTC

Yesterday's hot paper was Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights by Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang, and Omar Khattab. The paper (OK, the authors classify is as a "blog post", but it's paper-shaped) found that frontier models, in particular GPT-6 Astra, can both interpret and modify the raw weights of a machine learning model - literally a text description of the model containing a bunch of floating point numbers. I've been playing with one of the examples from the paper and I'm delighted to share that Qwen 3.8 27B running on my laptop can do this as well! Weight-Space Programming Here's the highlight from their abstract, describing impressive capabilities for GPT-6 Astra and coining the term Weight-Space Programming for when LLMs analyze and modify model weights: Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do. And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps.

Bliki: LLM Voice

Martin Fowler · Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知

Sometimes when I read a post, I get the growing feeling that I'm reading the output of an LLM. I can't necessarily define why, although there are the common tells (it's not the em-dashes, it's the load-bearing tapestries). As I do this my desire to read on atrophies, sometimes to the point of revulsion There are tools out there that claim to be able to tell the difference between LLM-written prose and the old-fashioned biological product. I'm wary of them, partly due skeptism about their accuracy, but also because it rather misses the point. The reaction to LLM-Voice is a human one, that sense that we are in an uncanny valley of prose. By the time I'd reach for a tool to tell me what I'm reading, it's already too late, even if it confidently tells me there's no LLM present. I'm also suspicious of my own ability to accurately recognize LLM voice. Language changes over time, so a common sign of age is complaining about the language of the youngs. I'm inclined to bristle at prose that talks about “adopting a new sales motion,” or “a sharp round-up of news”.

specialist_media · specialist · R5 · P5 · baseline

Why are good developers so wary of agentic development?

Martin Fowler · Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知

TL;DR Good developers’ caution about agentic development comes from knowing that built isn’t the same as working in production. I’ve been surprised by how many excellent developers have been hesitant to go all in on coding agents. These are people who usually try new ways of working before anyone else and in many cases invent new tools and practices that support building the application well. So why have we had so much reluctance? The easy (lazy?) answer is that they love writing code, or they’re worried about their jobs. I’m sure that’s true for some people, some of the time. And I know it is true for some of the developers I talk to but I always felt there was something else, another fear hiding behind those obvious ones. When we put together the Technology Radar every six months I try to block out a chunk of time for us to do an open space. In September, a discussion we had on agentic development, which pushed it to its limits, finally helped me see clearly what that fear is. Building it right Thoughtworkers care deeply about building the right thing and building it right.

Powering open infrastructure for autonomous agents

Google Cloud Blog · 2026-11-05 12:30 UTC

As AI shifts from human scale to agent scale, from systems of record to systems of action, and from simple requests to complex agentic workflows, the workload underneath your platform changes completely. An agent works in a continuous, stateful loop: It proposes an action, spins up subagents, executes code or tool calls inside a sandbox, and feeds the results back into the model for the next turn. Running that loop at scale requires the same open foundation and neutral governance that Kubernetes and the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) brought to containers in the 2010s. Today, we are announcing the donation of Agent Substrate, gVisor, and OpenRL, three open source projects that started at Google, to the CNCF following their acceptance last month into the CNCF Sandbox. To bring this open stack into managed production and accelerate it across TPUs and GPUs, we are also announcing that Agent Substrate has reached its 1.0 milestone and is now generally available as Agent Substrate on GKE.

Workflow SDK adds idempotent starts

Vercel Blog · Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知

The Workflow SDK's start() function can now admit a run and claim a hook in one atomic step. Duplicate workflow starts fail safely. The atomic start replaces the previous getHookByToken()-then-start() pattern, whose gap between the lookup and the start left a documented duplicate-start race. Subscribe to messages inside the run The claimed Hook exists from the moment the run is admitted, so resumeHook works even before the run begins executing, and early payloads are buffered and delivered in order. Inside the workflow, createHook({ token }) with the same token binds to the already-claimed hook: guaranteed, registering nothing new, adding no step, and resolving getConflict() to null. Idempotency with no extra code The token is the idempotency key, and it comes from your own domain: an order ID, an invoice ID, an import ID, or a request ID. The token alone guarantees idempotency. Exactly one run owns it, and a duplicate start() throws HookConflictError carrying the owner's conflictingRunId and never becomes a run.

Announcing the Workload Conformance Working Group

Kubernetes Blog · 2026-10-27 04:30 UTC

We are excited to announce that the Kubernetes community now has a Workload Conformance Working Group. The working group is writing a shared standard for how workloads behave at runtime on Kubernetes. To get it right, we need input from the people who build those workloads and from the people who run the clusters they're deployed on. Why workloads need a shared standard Certified Kubernetes tests the cluster, and Kubernetes AI Conformance tests whether a cluster can run AI and ML workloads. Nothing comparable exists for the workloads themselves, so cluster operators still check each application by hand before routine maintenance or a Kubernetes upgrade. The problems they find are familiar. A routine node drain is often how you discover that an application can't tolerate disruption. An upgrade can break an application that still depends on a removed API version. Others show up in day-to-day operation: workloads that ask for privileges they don't need, or reserve resources they never use. Kubernetes already documents much of this, including security and handling disruptions.

Making Failure Diagnosis Reliable with Pensive AI

Netflix TechBlog · 2026-10-26 17:04 UTC

By Praneeth Yenugutala, Victor Dusa, Anastasia Samoilova, Megan Ren, Justin Wei, Marcelo Mayworm At Netflix, data and machine learning practitioners run millions of workloads each day across orchestration systems and compute engines such as Titus, Spark, Trino, and Druid. On peak days, roughly 100,000 workloads fail. When workloads fail, the failure itself is only the beginning. Someone still needs to find the useful signal in several logs, decide whether the cause sits in their code or the platform, and determine whether to retry, reconfigure, or escalate. Even a small share of difficult failures can consume engineering time, waste compute, and interrupt critical data pipelines. Our first answer to that problem was Pensive, an auto-diagnosis and remediation system in Netflix’s data platform. Pensive collected logs from failed workloads, used regular expressions and hand-authored Java rules to extract and classify errors, then passed retry or remediation guidance to products such as Maestro. It made ~ 50% of failures self-service and, in some cases, automatic.

Samartha Chandrashekar & Nick Parker You click play on a Friday night, and in the second that follows, dozens of services answer in milliseconds. Most of them run on Titus, our internal container platform. Titus is, in essence, a Kubernetes-based container hosting platform: we keep both the control plane and the data plane (the container hosts that actually run containers) patched and up to date, so application teams get a consistent and reliable container experience. They hand us a container, and we run it, with no host, cluster, or kernel to own. Titus launches millions of containers every week across tens of thousands of EC2 instances in multiple AWS regions. It is multi-tenant by default: many containers from many teams share each host. That density is what makes container compute efficient, and it is why Titus has been the default home for so much of Netflix’s compute for years. For most workloads, sharing a host works well. For a few, it does not, and those few include some of the most demanding real-time systems we run.

The useful question is not only “Why is the Pod pending?” It is first “Has Kueue admitted the Workload?” The Kueue plugin for Headlamp brings that investigation into the Headlamp UI. Instead of reconstructing the admission path from several commands and large YAML objects, you can begin with the Workload, read its condition message, and follow links through the LocalQueue, ClusterQueue, ResourceFlavor, and Cohort. This article follows that Headlamp-first path. The command line appears only in a short optional section for reproducing the example. Before you begin You need a Kubernetes cluster with Kueue installed, a Headlamp installation, and the 0.1.0-alpha Kueue plugin.

The Shift to cgroup v2 in Kubernetes: What You Need to Know

Kubernetes Blog · 2026-10-06 18:00 UTC

In Linux, cgroups (control groups) are a kernel feature used for managing system resources. Kubernetes uses cgroups to allocate resources like CPU and memory to containers, ensuring that applications run smoothly without interfering with each other. With the release of Kubernetes v1.31, support for v1 cgroup management moved into maintenance mode. Support for v2 cgroup management has been stable since Kubernetes v1.25. Compared with cgroup v1, cgroup v2 provides a single unified hierarchy, a more consistent interface, and a stronger foundation for resource isolation and modern resource-management features. Deprecation of cgroup v1 Kubernetes has deprecated cgroup v1. Starting with Kubernetes v1.35, failCgroupV1 defaults to true, so the kubelet does not start on a cgroup v1 node by default. Administrators can temporarily set failCgroupV1: false in the kubelet configuration file, but removal will follow the Kubernetes deprecation policy. Further removal work is tracked in KEP-5573: Remove cgroup v1 support. If you are still on a release older than v1.

Scaling Kubernetes Workloads with Node Swap

Kubernetes Blog · 2026-10-05 18:00 UTC

Memory is often the first hard limit a Kubernetes cluster hits. Nodes run out of RAM long before they run out of CPU, and the new wave of agentic AI workloads makes this worse. These workloads demand large memory footprints to start up and run untrusted code, then sit idle waiting for the next prompt. That idle but resident memory is expensive, and it caps how many pods a node can hold. This is where swap helps. Kubernetes support for running nodes with swap enabled reached General Availability in v1.34, and by backing that swap with fast NVMe solid state drives (SSDs), a node can page out dormant memory and pack in far more pods. This post explains how we benchmarked that approach across three workloads, including CI/CD kernel builds, sandboxed headless browsers, and isolated Python runtimes; we found density gains of up to 3×, often with little or no latency cost.

Spotlight on SIG Apps

Kubernetes Blog · 2026-09-22 18:00 UTC

As Kubernetes adoption has grown, the conversation has shifted beyond running containers to managing increasingly complex application lifecycles. Modern platforms support stateless web services, stateful databases, batch processing, AI workloads, and platform services. At the same time, they must remain reliable during upgrades, scaling events, and infrastructure failures. Every Kubernetes user relies on SIG Apps, whether they realize it or not. Deployments, StatefulSets, DaemonSets, Jobs, and CronJobs form the foundation of how applications are deployed, updated, scaled, and operated across the Kubernetes ecosystem. SIG Apps is focused on improving workload resilience, refining application lifecycle management, and addressing the operational challenges that emerge when applications encounter node failures, rollout disruptions, and increasingly complex infrastructure environments.

Autonomous Airships Keep Tabs on Energy Infrastructure

IEEE Spectrum Aerospace · 2026-10-29 14:00 UTC

Inspecting thousands of kilometers of power lines, pipelines, or rail tracks is an expensive and time-consuming business. It’s typically done by helicopters, which are costly, noisy, and polluting. French startup HyLight thinks uncrewed airships could be a cheaper, more environmentally friendly alternative. The company has developed a 12-meter-long blimp powered by a hydrogen fuel cell capable of staying airborne for up to 10 hours and traveling 350 kilometers per day. The airship carries an array of sensors for inspection, including high-precision cameras, lidar, and methane detectors. HyLight uses AI models (some developed in-house, some off the shelf) to automatically analyze collected data and identify more than 50 types of maintenance issues. The French civil aviation authority and the European Union Aviation Safety Agency have both granted permission for HyLight’s airships—which have so far logged more than 750 flight hours—to operate beyond visual line of sight.

How Beta Technologies Is Clearing the Runway for Electric Flight

IEEE Spectrum Aerospace · 2026-10-28 13:00 UTC

In the cockpit of Beta Technologies’ Alia CX300, pilot Chris Caputo steers onto Runway 33 at Patrick Leahy Burlington International Airport in Vermont. Cleared for takeoff, he releases the brakes and nudges the throttle forward. At the back of the aircraft, the five-blade pusher propeller snaps awake, and the Alia bolts forward. There’s no shriek of a turbofan spooling up, no shudder of a piston engine, and no wait for thrust. Just the low hum of an electric motor and a shove of instant acceleration. Within a few seconds, we’re at 85 knots (almost 160 kilometers per hour), and Caputo rotates the nose upward. The runway drops abruptly away as we climb. Gaining speed and altitude, we head northwest over Lake Champlain. Through the wraparound canopy, I watch the hunched shoulders of Vermont’s Green Mountains shrink under the right wing, with New York’s taller Adirondacks to the left. Caputo, a former Air Force fighter pilot, flicks the control stick hard left, then right.

Your Robot’s Safety Functions Already Work. What If the Input Lies?

IEEE Spectrum Robotics · 2026-10-27 16:14 UTC

This article is brought to you by VicOne. A mobile robot slows for someone in a hallway. A collaborative arm eases its movement as a worker approaches. A humanoid pauses to let a person pass. Each response depends on information about the robot or its surroundings: a distance reading, a position estimate, or a stop signal. But what happens when one of those inputs is wrong, and the robot still responds exactly as designed? The mobile robot reads the hallway as clear while someone is still there. The arm estimates that the worker is farther away. The humanoid does not receive a stop signal as a person crosses its path. In each case, a fault could cause that mismatch. So could deliberate manipulation. At VicOne LAB R7, we examine how manipulated inputs can change robot behavior — and what that means for the systems meant to keep people safe. How an untrusted input can change a robot’s behavior A robot does more than measure its surroundings. It may interpret what it sees and hears to decide what to do next. Information placed in its environment can therefore influence its actions.

Will Fiber-Optic Cables Finally Get Made in Orbit?

IEEE Spectrum Aerospace · 2026-10-26 12:00 UTC

In a lab in Luxembourg in 2024, engineers at Flawless Photonics unpacked a spool of glass fiber that had just returned from the International Space Station (ISS). As they threaded it onto their rewinding machine, the machine jammed—as happens sometimes—and they braced for the usual outcome: The fiber would snap. This time, though, nothing broke. It was an early hint that their experiment might have been successful. The Flawless Photonics team had set out to draw fibers of a heavy-metal fluoride glass called ZBLAN—named for its other components of zirconium, barium, lanthanum, aluminum, and sodium (chemical symbol Na)—in microgravity, aiming to achieve superior optical and physical properties. “We realized, wow, that fiber is much stronger than the stuff we had produced on Earth,” says Hubert Moser, the company’s cofounder and CTO. The Robot I Didn’t Expect to Build

IEEE Spectrum Robotics · 2026-10-19 13:00 UTC

Agility Robotics, the company I cofounded out of my robotics lab at Oregon State University in 2015, has just launched Digit 5. It’s designed to be the first humanoid robot that can safely and economically do useful work at scale, allowing us to bring tens of thousands of humanoid workers into the real world. Engineered to lift 23-kilogram bins onto high shelves and with a battery that can run for 90 minutes on a 9-minute charge, Digit 5’s goal is to handle heavy warehouse tasks shift after shift, filling the need for labor in jobs that are too physically stressful or too dull for humans to want to do. Digit 5 is what Agility has been working toward for over a decade. But the robot is heavy and bulky, lacking the graceful natural motion of its predecessors, and it’s farther than I thought possible from the robot I dreamed of building when I started this company. To deliver a useful commercial product, Agility has taken a path that is very different from what I first imagined.

In one month, the European Space Agency’s Hera mission will make history. NASA’s Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) mission slammed into Dimorphos in 2022, and now Hera will provide a follow-up view of the mission’s resulting handiwork. The European Space Agency (ESA) recently released a thought-provoking look at the perspectives of Hera and what an astronaut might see from the surface of the asteroids as the mission speeds by. But what would it be like to hitch a ride aboard Hera? Launched on a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket from Cape Canaveral, Fla., on 7 October 2024, Hera is ESA’s first Space Safety Programme-class mission. The spacecraft took just over two years to reach its destination. Even now, the pair of asteroids is little more than a few pixels across in Hera’s view. The mission imaged Didymos in July 2026.
